title: Part VIII — LEADERSHIP: The Chief Architect's Agenda
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published page (posts/part-8-intro/index.md) and its former spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces; one spec paragraph per unit of the page, in the page's order. Intent outcome, AC-1 to AC-3 and role are copied unchanged from the post's entry in journal-spec.json; the introduction realises Part VIII's opening (hook, bridge, roadmap) from the same file. The journal spec gives this post no thesis, so the thesis and its three supporting claims are written here from the part's thesis and flow. The five callouts (IN THIS PART, WHY THE BUSINESS CARES, WHY ARCHITECTS SHOULD CARE, KEY POINTS, FAILURE PATTERNS) stand before the first paragraph and are kept as the house format; the KEY POINTS callout carries the part's claim in three bullets and the IN THIS PART callout names the five chapter subjects in reading order. know: Part VIII's argument: the hard problems of a marketplace group are problems of change, not of design, so change is sequenced by risk to liquidity, every capability gets one owning team, AI proposes while the structured systems decide, and the platform is steered by fitness functions.
The five chapters in reading order, the question each answers and when to read it, and the Veldmark decisions of 2027 they follow.

audience.who: Chief and group architects, CTOs, principal engineers and engineering leaders who must sequence platform change across acquired marketplaces, assign ownership and keep the result coherent over years (the journal's readers), who have read Part VII and are about to start Part VIII, or who arrive with a leadership problem in hand and want the chapter that answers it.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine and Kubernetes are; how to make and defend an architecture decision; what a monolith, a rewrite and a cut-over are.

Part VII's platform: the listing event contract, the ML platform and model registry, the tenancy model with its release rings, and journey reliability (event-driven-listings, ml-platform, multi-country-platforms, reliability-and-scale); Part IV's search platform (search-architecture); Part I's context map (bounded-contexts); Part II's taxonomy and attribute schemas; Part VI's paid bumps; liquidity as buyers finding listings and sellers getting contacts.
The fifteen named failure patterns, among them Deal-Shaped Architecture, The Forced Fit and Set-and-Forget AI (where-listing-systems-go-wrong).

Veldmark in outline: a fictional group of four brands (Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly, Keybridge), Casavista as Hearthly's Spanish acquisition, the Common Ground program, Ingrid Halvorsen its Group Chief Architect, Yardstick, Tradeyard's PHP monolith, the architecture advice forum, and the people table, among them Yara Mendes (Platform Engineering) (meet-veldmark and earlier chapters).
does_not_know: Integration option, consolidation sequence, synergy ledger and dis-synergies (owned by platform-consolidation; the page names the synergy ledger only as a Veldmark decision 'in place of spreadsheets', and glosses Keybridge's option 'federated under group controls' as 'sharing finance and security only').

Stream-aligned and platform teams, decision rights and the advice process (owned by organizing-marketplace-engineering; the KEY POINTS callout says 'platform teams earn their tenants by being worth adopting' and 'an open, recorded advice process rather than a review board that owns nothing').

Strangling a monolith behind seams, stage gates and relevance parity (owned by modernization-and-migration; the KEY POINTS callout says 'slice by slice behind a seam' and 'gate every step on measured outcomes with a rollback answer').
The AI control layer and the AI use register (owned by ai-in-listing-systems; the KEY POINTS callout says 'let AI propose while the structured systems decide').

Stressor analysis and marketplace fitness functions (owned by long-term-evolution; the KEY POINTS callout glosses stressors as 'new owners, laws, channels'; fitness functions are named as what the chapter builds).

thesis.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?
thesis.claim: Part VIII argues that the hard problems of a marketplace group are problems of change, not of design: change is sequenced by risk to liquidity and each step gated on measured outcomes with a rollback answer, every journey, bounded context and shared capability gets exactly one owning team with cross-brand decisions made through a recorded advice process, AI proposes while the structured systems decide, and the platform is steered by fitness functions rather than program milestones; its five chapters are read in the order each acts on what the one before decided: consolidation chooses what to share, organization assigns owners, migration uses those owners to retire the monolith, AI builds on the changed platform, and long-term evolution tests every decision over a decade.
thesis.disputed_by: The program view of transformation, in which the target architecture is the hard part and the rest is execution on the deal's timetable, so the leadership chapters are independent management topics a reader may consult in any order.
thesis.so_what: A reader who accepts it reads the consolidation chapter first, or opens the one chapter that answers the leadership problem in front of them, and judges any change plan by what it changes first, who owns it, how it will be known to work and what must stay true.
thesis.how_why: Each chapter's input is the previous chapter's output: organizing-marketplace-engineering assigns owners to the capabilities consolidation chose to share, every migration slice needs an owning team from the target organization, the AI control layer uses the centrally owned gateway, the model registry and the services migration moved out of the monolith, and long-term evolution sorts all of these decisions into what lasts and what is replaced. Veldmark's 2027 problems were problems of change: by October 2027 the Casavista deal had delivered €9.6 million of €18 million in promised synergies, and Common Ground (€140 million over 2027–2030) must retire Yardstick by the end of 2029.

supporting_claims.claim: The five chapters are read in the order each acts on what the one before decided, and each is the chapter to open first for a recognizable symptom.
Each chapter builds on a design from an earlier part, and Part IX tests the part's argument against publicly documented marketplace groups.
Veldmark's 2027 decisions, shaped by Ingrid Halvorsen and taken by the CTO, the board and the advice forum, move Common Ground from plan to practice, and each is the material of one or two chapters.

flow.rationale: The page opens on the step after Part VII (a designed platform that a group assembled by acquisition has only on paper), states the part's claim (change, not design, is the hard problem), then gives the reading order with the reason for it and narrows to one row per chapter with the symptom that sends a reader there. It widens once to say which earlier designs the chapters build on and where Part IX takes the argument, shows Veldmark's 2027 decisions, and ends with a short synthesis, the part's test and the hand-off to the first chapter. The order is given before the table because the rows read as a sequence only once the reader knows each chapter acts on what the one before decided; the connection section follows the table because it names what each listed chapter builds on; the Veldmark section follows because its decisions are what the chapters design; the conclusion comes last and holds no new material. Put Veldmark first and its decisions arrive before the reader knows which chapter treats each; put the connection first and it names consolidation, migration and owning teams before the reader has met the chapters that treat them.

The part's claim is that the hard problems of a marketplace group are problems of change, not of design: a group assembled by acquisition has platforms in several copies, teams that follow old org charts, a monolith that still bills sellers for bumps and unknown future owners and regulators, and the architect changes all of this while buyers keep finding things and sellers keep getting contacts.
